analysis.one_liner: Ends corporate tax deductions for million-dollar pay to contractors, former executives, and pass-through recipients.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced May 1, 2025 with 22 Democratic cosponsors and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Current tax law stops companies from deducting executive pay over $1 million per person, but the rule only covers employees, and companies have worked around it by paying advisers, contractors, and former executives outside that rule. This bill would extend the $1 million deduction cap to anyone performing services for a company, bring back executives and top-paid officers from earlier years, tighten the definition of which corporations are covered, and let the Treasury write rules against routing pay through other entities. The effect is that large public companies would pay more in taxes on pay packages above $1 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways: companies would no longer be able to deduct pay above $1 million paid to contractors, former executives, or people paid through pass-through entities, which would raise federal revenue and make the tax code less tilted toward the highest-paid individuals. Workers whose compensation is set in comparison to executive pay could also benefit if the cap changes how companies structure top pay.

how_it_helps.text: The bill changes section 162(m) of the tax code so the $1 million deduction cap applies to any individual who performs services for the company, not just employees, closing a route companies use to deduct large payments to non-employee advisers and contractors.

It extends the cap to cover former principal executive and financial officers and the three highest-paid officers from years after 2016, closing a 'former employee' loophole that lets departing executives keep deductible pay packages.
It would apply to any corporation that was required to file reports with the SEC at any time in the past three years, so companies could not dodge the rule by briefly going private.
It gives the Treasury Secretary authority to write rules preventing companies from avoiding the cap by routing compensation through pass-through or other entities.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded corporations and their most highly paid individuals — executives, former executives, and high-priced contractors receiving pay above $1 million — who would lose the tax deduction on amounts above that level, raising those companies' tax bills.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large public corporations and top earners

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes on the affected companies, and a good-faith objection is that higher corporate tax costs can mean less money for investment, hiring, or wages.

Compliance would get more complicated: companies would have to track who counts as a 'covered individual' going back to 2016 and 2020 look-back periods, which imposes new accounting and record-keeping burdens.
The bill gives the Treasury broad regulatory authority, including rules to prevent avoidance, which means the final reach of the rule depends on how future administrations write the regulations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a somewhat higher tax bill for a few hundred large corporations and their top earners, in exchange for revenue and a less lopsided tax code. The compliance complexity and look-back rules are real costs for affected firms but fall on their payroll and tax departments, not on ordinary workers. The main weakness is design rather than substance — a rule that applies to individual pay above $1 million leaves room for compensation to be restructured into other forms, which is partly why the bill includes regulatory authority to police avoidance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has not taken it up.

narrative.text: Representative Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on May 1, 2025, joined by 22 Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and no further action appears in the bill's history.
All 22 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large public corporations and highly paid executives, who keep the current deduction for pay above $1 million paid to contractors and former executives while the bill sits without a hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations and top executives keep the deduction

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the $1 million deduction cap beyond employees and close related loopholes.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor action on the bill since it was referred in May 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors are Democrats and the bill sits in a committee run by the Republican majority, with no Republican support in the record.

industries.note: These companies would lose the deduction on pay above $1 million paid to contractors, former executives, and pass-through recipients, increasing their tax bills. Their interest in keeping the current broader deduction runs against ordinary taxpayers, who would bear more of the tax burden without the bill.

industries.industry: Highly paid executives and non-employee advisers (contractors, consultants, fund managers paid through pass-throughs)
industries.note: Individuals receiving more than $1 million in pay from a public company would see that excess no longer deductible for the company, which typically pressures companies to restrain or restructure such pay. Their preference for the status quo comes at the cost of a narrower tax base for everyone else.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to change the corporate tax code move only if the Ways and Means Committee takes them up, and this one has a single-party sponsor list and no committee action months after referral. Unless tax legislation moves and its provisions are attached, the bill is likely to sit in committee for the rest of this Congress.
